title: Robbins Mounds, Boone County
summary: In Boone County, the Robbins Mound Complex was a pair of Adena burial mounds that University of Kentucky crews excavated during the Great Depression.
bodyMarkdown:
The [Robbins Mound Complex](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Robbins-Mound-Complex.aspx) was a pair of burial mounds built on an upland ridge crest in [Boone County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Boone_County,_Kentucky). Their builders belonged to the [Adena culture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Adena_culture), and the Kentucky Archaeological Survey dates the mounds to the Middle [Woodland period](https://grokipedia.com/page/Woodland_period), about 200 BC to AD 500; other classifications put Adena in the Early Woodland. Archaeologists recorded them as sites 15Be3 and 15Be14.

What survives of them is mostly knowledge. In 1939, during the Great Depression, the University of Kentucky hired local men to excavate the mounds, part of the relief-era archaeology that also explored sites such as [Mount Horeb](/stories/mount-horeb-earthworks/). After clearing the trees, the crews dug one five-foot square at a time, keeping careful records that let archaeologists reconstruct how the larger mound was built.

That mound, 15Be3, stood about 20 feet high and 131 feet across. It began with a circular enclosure about 30 feet across whose walls leaned slightly outward. There was no sign of a roof, and archaeologists think it worked as a screen that hid ritual activity from view. A large area of burned soil inside probably came from a fire tied to those rituals.

While the enclosure was still in use, people raised a small mound inside it and buried the cremated remains of several individuals.

Over time, the mound grew in stages. The excavators found 52 tombs built of logs and bark, some holding more than one person. At least 100 people were buried in the mound, 89 of them in those tombs. Men and women were represented in roughly equal numbers, both young and older adults, and some tombs had been opened and reused.

Later burials were placed in pits before a final cap of earth covered the whole.

The smaller mound, 15Be14, lay about 100 feet to the south. Plowing had reduced it to about two feet high by the time it was excavated. Its diameter could not be measured, and it held a single burial feature, probably a log-lined tomb, suggesting that it was used for a much shorter time.

The reused tombs and the stages of building show people returning to the same place over a long time to bury their dead. Adena peoples lived in small, dispersed communities, and their mounds are found across the region, as at [Ashland's Adena Mounds](/stories/ashlands-adena-mounds/).

## Kentucky today

The Robbins mounds are known today mainly through the 1939 excavation records, which the [Kentucky Heritage Council](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Robbins-Mound-Complex.aspx) summarizes for the public. That record is what lets this Boone County community of the dead be described at all.
